To attain equality the velocity is nonnegative off the zero and equals (L/B)sqrt(sigma/zeta); it also vanishes almost everywhere on the zero level set. Taylor's theorem at the C² nonnegative interior minimum gives a velocity bounded by a multiple of distance to c, preventing a finite crossing. Integrating the positive regularized speed gives the exact budget and E=J_epsilon K_epsilon/B, so dominated convergence proves sharpness without attainment. Comparison near c with quadratic coefficients A±delta gives the logarithmic coefficient for a nondegenerate quadratic zero only. To test the claim for all minimizing sequences, rescale any bounded-time subsequence to [0,1], where times are bounded away from zero by B/max(sigma). The transform x↦integral_a^x sqrt(zeta) turns the weighted energy into a time-scaled squared derivative norm; compactness and lower semicontinuity then give a limiting admissible optimizer, a contradiction. More generally, the separated equality-time integral is locally finite iff p<2, under the stated isolated-zero power law and continuity/positivity away from c; its inverse gives an absolutely continuous path when finite. For the ring, differentiating stationarity at zero gives pi'=(-2,1,1)/9 and the clockwise current derivative 1/3. value.rationale: The positive-weight formula alone can suggest a finite optimal protocol even when the required physical time diverges. The result resolves this boundary for a physically realizable simple Markov model, distinguishes sharp infimum from an achieved optimum, and quantifies how the time required for one explicit exactly budgeted approximation grows. The critical vanishing order and all-sequence obstruction are usable diagnostics for leading-order optimization; no exact finite-speed physical guarantee is made.
